decisions.identity_check: Gareth Heyes is identified as a web/browser/XSS security researcher at PortSwigger (the organization behind Burp Suite). The PortSwigger researcher profile (https://portswigger.net/research/gareth-heyes), fetched directly, lists his role as Researcher and describes him as best known for AngularJS sandbox escape work and XSS vectors; this is consistent with the person record's primary_focus (browser/XSS/CSP vulnerabilities) and the social handle @garethheyes (https://x.com/garethheyes). No same-name ambiguity was encountered in fetched sources; the name appears distinctive within the web-security field. Identity is confirmed by the convergence of employer (PortSwigger), specialization (XSS / AngularJS / CSS), and social handle.

items.claim: On 11 May 2017 Gareth Heyes published 'DOM based AngularJS sandbox escapes'. The PortSwigger researcher profile states he is best known for AngularJS sandbox escape work and XSS vector creation, indicating DOM-based XSS and JavaScript sandbox escape as his established research area.
items.growth_signal: This is the earliest of his self-selected representative works and establishes DOM-based XSS / JavaScript sandbox escape against a widely-deployed framework as the baseline competence against which his later method transitions are measured. The profile framing ('creating ... XSS vectors') is consistent with repeated vector production and a publication habit as the growth mechanism, rather than an innate-ability explanation.
items.short_quote: probably best known for smashing the AngularJS sandbox to pieces and creating super-elegant XSS vectors

items.claim: On 5 December 2023 Gareth Heyes published 'Blind CSS Exfiltration: exfiltrate unknown web pages', a technique that uses CSS to exfiltrate content from web pages.
items.growth_signal: A roughly six-year interval separates this from his 2017 AngularJS/XSS work, and the topic moves the offensive medium from JavaScript execution to CSS. Read against the 2017 baseline, this supports an inferred method transition (转向) toward CSS as an exfiltration vector. The transition itself is inferred from the dated publication contrast; no first-person statement of a deliberate decision was found.

items.claim: On 7 August 2024 Gareth Heyes published 'Splitting the email atom: exploiting parsers to bypass access controls', extending the attack surface to email parsers and access-control bypasses.
items.growth_signal: Relative to the 2023 web-page/CSS work, the 2024 target moves from browser/web-page context to email-client parsers. The 2023-to-2024 sequence is consistent with reapplying markup/parser techniques to a different parser domain, i.e. an expansion of attack surface (攻击面扩展). The expansion is inferred from the topic sequence, not from a stated decision.

items.claim: On 6 August 2026 Gareth Heyes published 'CSS: the bomb inside your inbox', combining the CSS-offensive thread with the email/inbox thread in a single attack vector.
items.growth_signal: This work converges the CSS-exfiltration thread (2023) and the email-parser thread (2024) into one inbox attack. It represents a continuation-and-synthesis of the prior method transitions rather than a new independent direction, consistent with consolidation of earlier lines of work.

items.claim: As presented on the PortSwigger researcher profile (profile content current through at least 2026-08-06), Gareth Heyes's role is Researcher at PortSwigger; the profile credits him as creator of PortSwigger's XSS Cheat Sheet, developer of the Hackvertor BApp extension, and author of the book 'JavaScript for hackers'.
items.growth_signal: A sustained accumulation of reusable offensive tooling and reference material (XSS Cheat Sheet, Hackvertor, a book) alongside original research points to tool-building (工具建设) and publication (公开发表) as recurring components of his research practice. The deliberateness of this pattern is inferred from the accumulation; no first-person statement of intent was found.

contradictions: No mutually conflicting fetched primary sources were identified. The PortSwigger researcher profile is the sole fetched primary source and is internally consistent.
gaps: No fetched source documents when Gareth Heyes joined PortSwigger or any prior employment; only his current role (Researcher at PortSwigger) is documented.
Early-career origin — how and when Heyes began in security — is not documented in any fetched source.

Book 'JavaScript for hackers': authorship is documented on the PortSwigger profile, but the publisher and publication date were not confirmed. Wiley product pages returned HTTP 404 for the ISBNs tried; the No Starch Press catalog search did not return the title; only an unauthoritative search-result snippet suggested Wiley, which was not adopted.

An unattributed, model-generated search response (which self-reported having no search tool and sharing training-data guesses) stated that Heyes works at Google on XSS prevention. This is not corroborated by any fetched primary source and conflicts with the PortSwigger profile identifying his employer as PortSwigger; it is treated as unverified, not as a sourced claim.

Black Hat talk titles and years: the person record lists 'Black Hat US/EU' as conference evidence, but no specific briefing was verified through a fetched primary source. The blackhat.com speaker page returned HTTP 403, and no fetched content confirmed any individual talk.
sla.ckers.org forum participation is mentioned only in search summaries, not in any fetched primary source.

Hackvertor's earlier history as a standalone web tool predating the Burp Suite (BApp) extension is described only in non-fetched secondary/search content; only the BApp extension form is documented on the PortSwigger profile.

No first-person writeup, interview, or talk material was found in which Heyes states a deliberate career or method-shift decision, or its rationale. The method-transition framing (XSS / JS-sandbox to CSS to email) is inferred from the dated publication sequence, not from his own stated reasoning.
